identification.summary: Kaspersky describes Angry Likho (called Sticky Werewolf by some vendors) as an APT group it has monitored since 2023, which it placed in its Likho cluster because it strongly resembles Awaken Likho [S1]. BI.ZONE first documented Sticky Werewolf in October 2023 and said it had been active since April 2023 with at least 30 attacks on government organizations in Russia and Belarus [S4][S5]. Kaspersky reports its 2025 attacks deliver the Lumma Stealer via spear-phishing with archives containing shortcut (LNK) files and a lure document [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: April 2023 (BI.ZONE and Morphisec: active since April 2023); first publicly documented October 2023 [S4][S3][S5].
identification.notes: Kaspersky name: Angry Likho; Sticky Werewolf is the name used by other vendors (BI.ZONE, Morphisec) [S1][S3]. Kaspersky treats it as a separate cluster from Awaken Likho while noting strong resemblance [S1]. Whether the 2023-2024 Sticky Werewolf reporting and the 2025 Angry Likho reporting describe exactly the same operator is stated by Kaspersky and press coverage but the vendors' own cluster boundaries were not verified against primary documents [S1][S2].

attribution.confidence: Not attributed to a state by any source gathered. Morphisec says the group's origin is unclear and no definitive evidence points to a specific national origin, noting only a possible but unconfirmed link to a pro-Ukrainian cyberespionage group or hacktivists [S3][S6].
attribution.basis: Targeting concentrated in Russia and Belarus [S1][S4]. Kaspersky reportedly judged the operators likely native Russian speakers based on the fluent Russian of the bait files (as relayed in search-result summaries of the Securelist report) [S1]. These are vendor assessments, not government attribution.

objectives: Kaspersky says attacks focus on employees of large organizations, including government agencies and their contractors, and Lumma harvests browser data, banking details, credentials and cryptowallet files [S1][S2]. Morphisec assessed that recent techniques suggest espionage and data exfiltration intent [S3]. Coverage also emphasizes a financial-theft dimension, so the objective mix is unresolved [S2].

targeting.notes: BI.ZONE: government organizations in Russia and Belarus in 2023 [S4][S5]. Morphisec (June 2024): a pharmaceutical company, a Russian microbiology and vaccine institute, and the aviation sector, with email lures impersonating an executive at a Moscow aircraft and spacecraft firm [S3][S6]. Kaspersky (Feb 2025): hundreds of victims in Russia, several in Belarus, additional incidents elsewhere assessed as likely incidental; main targets are in Russia and Belarus [S1].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with RAR or password-protected archives containing LNK files and decoy documents; LNKs fetch payloads from WebDAV servers, an earlier chain used gofile.io download links [S3][S6]. Kaspersky reports Lumma Stealer delivered in 2025, including via an NSIS self-extracting archive named FrameworkSurvivor.exe, with sandbox/emulator checks that exit or wait 10,000 ms, a technique also seen in Awaken Likho implants [S1][S2]. Kaspersky describes a compact infrastructure, a limited range of implants and reliance on readily available malicious utilities from darknet forums [S1]. Earlier Sticky Werewolf payloads reported by BI.ZONE and Morphisec: NetWire (2023), DarkTrack, MetaStealer, Rhadamanthys Stealer and Ozone RAT, with a variant of the CypherIT cryptor [S5][S3][S6].

campaigns.summary: Archive attachments with LNK files pulling payloads from WebDAV servers, delivering Rhadamanthys Stealer and Ozone RAT; aviation lure impersonated an executive at a Moscow aerospace firm.

campaigns.name: Angry Likho Lumma wave (Kaspersky)
campaigns.summary: Standardized spear-phishing with RAR archives and LNK files delivering Lumma Stealer; new FrameworkSurvivor.exe NSIS delivery; hundreds of victims in Russia and several in Belarus.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed cluster tracked as Angry Likho (Kaspersky) and Sticky Werewolf (BI.ZONE, Morphisec); origin disputed or unknown [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.capability: Archive and LNK phishing chains, WebDAV payload hosting, commodity stealers and RATs (Lumma, Rhadamanthys, Ozone RAT, NetWire, DarkTrack) and NSIS packaging [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compact infrastructure per Kaspersky [S1]; WebDAV servers and gofile.io links used for payload delivery [S3][S6]. Specific indicators not gathered.
diamond.victim: Government agencies and contractors, aviation, pharmaceutical and vaccine research organizations in Russia and Belarus [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targets sit inside Russia and Belarus; Morphisec notes a possible but unconfirmed pro-Ukrainian link, which remains uncertain [S6][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached by email attachments; Windows shortcut (LNK) files, WebDAV and self-extracting archives abused; browser-stored credentials and cryptowallet files targeted [S1][S3].

gaps: Could not open the primary Securelist, Morphisec, BI.ZONE or The Hacker News pages (fetch failed); statements rely on search-result excerpts of those documents and should be verified against them.

Sponsor, nationality and motive are unresolved: Morphisec cites only a possible, unconfirmed pro-Ukrainian link and says no definitive origin evidence exists; Kaspersky's Russian-speaker judgment is only indirect evidence. An earlier F6 'pro-Ukrainian' characterization was not verified.
Exact relationship to Awaken Likho (shared tooling or single operator) is raised by Kaspersky but not resolved [S1].
Records from this encyclopedia list country RU; no cited source supports Russian state origin, so that field should be reviewed.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name located; no IOCs, C2 domains or hashes gathered.
Activity after February 2025 not found in searches.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways and user endpoints at government, defense-industrial, aviation and pharmaceutical organizations are the exposed terrain, but the cited victims are Russian and Belarusian, so direct US exposure is not shown in sources [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Capability is commodity: purchased stealers and RATs, LNK/archive lures, compact infrastructure [S1]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with archive, then LNK, then WebDAV or NSIS payload, then Lumma or RAT, then credential and wallet theft [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued phishing waves against Russia and Belarus government and industry. MDCOA is retargeting at other aviation or pharmaceutical organizations using the same lures. Candidate indicators: LNK files inside RAR archives launching executables from WebDAV paths, FrameworkSurvivor.exe, sandbox sleep of 10,000 ms [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a low-sophistication commodity-malware cluster; track vendor reporting for spread beyond Russia and Belarus [S1]. (2) Authorities: no US-relevant victimization shown; any defensive action stays within owned networks. (3) Mission assurance: block or alert on LNK-in-archive attachments and outbound WebDAV from user endpoints; protect browser-stored credentials [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through standard CTI channels if observed; attribution is unresolved, so avoid naming a sponsor.

provenance.importedSummary: Angry Likho is an APT group that has been active since 2023, primarily targeting large organizations and government agencies in Russia and Belarus. Their attacks typically involve spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments, such as RAR archives, and utilize a known payload, the Lumma stealer, for data exfiltration. The group employs a compact infrastructure and has been linked to espionage activities, particularly in sectors like aviation and pharmaceuticals. Their operations have shown a focus on collecting sensitive information, including cryptowallet files and user credentials.
